newsitem.title: INDIA: No SIA replacement in India Tata airline deal yet.
newsitem.headline: No SIA replacement in India Tata airline deal yet.

text.p: India's Tata Industries said on Thursday it had not yet sought replacements to help rescue a $600 million tie-up with Singapore Airlines to launch a domestic venture, now blocked by an aviation policy change.
"We have still not decided a strategy," S. Ramakrishnan, vice-president in charge of the Tata-SIA project, told Reuters. "We do not have any alternate plan yet."
Prime H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet on Tuesday forbade foreign airlines from holding equity in the domestic sector, in a move which appears to rule out the deal between Tata and SIA.
"It's not a great signal for foreign investors," said Ramakrishnan, adding that Tata had not yet received official notification of the federal decision.
"At the time the deal was put together, it was in line with the rules, which have been changed twice or thrice since then."
SIA and Tata Industries Ltd submitted their proposal to launch a joint airline in February 1995. Tata planned to hold a 60 percent stake, with SIA owning the rest.
Since then, it has languished with the government, ensnared in a high-stakes battle whether to permit foreign investment in the civil aviation sector.

Ramakrishnan had told Reuters on Tuesday that Tata would attempt to salvage the deal somehow, but was still undecided whether to restructure it in line with the new policy or simply give it up altogether.
However, he refused to comment on whether Tata had been approached by other suitors seeking to replace Singapore Airlines.

Tuesday's decision seemed a victory for Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim, who has waged a high-profile battle to protect the state-owned airlines -- Indian Airlines on domestic routes and Air-India on international routes -- from foreign competition.

The cabinet also upheld a rule, set in January, limiting foreign firms which are not airlines to 40 percent equity stakes in domestic airlines. Non-resident Indians can hold stakes of up to 100 percent.
Foreign investors, whether or not they are airlines, which currently hold stakes in Indian airlines will have to conform to the rules.
Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways each have 20 percent stakes, valued at $4 million, in India's Jet Airways.
India began opening its aviation sector as part of an economic liberalisation programme launched in 1991.
"We have always maintained that there is enough space for all the players in the domestic sector," Ramakrishnan said,
